I am interested in the mathematical study of programming languages. In particular, I study the application of logic and category theory to the design and implementation of provably correct software.

fr:title.text: Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
We present Dependent Lambek Calculus, a domain-specific dependent type theory for verified parsing and formal grammar theory. In Dependent Lambek Calculus, linear types are used as a syntax for formal grammars, and parsers can be written as linear terms. The linear typing restriction provides a form of intrinsic verification that a parser yields only valid parse trees for the input string. We demonstrate the expressivity of this system by showing that the combination of inductive linear types and dependency on non-linear data can be used to encode commonly used grammar formalisms such as regular and context-free grammars as well as traces of various types of automata. Using these encodings, we define parsers for regular expressions using deterministic automata, as well as examples of verified parsers of context-free grammars.
We present a denotational semantics of our type theory that interprets the types as a mathematical notion of formal grammars. Based on this denotational semantics, we have made a prototype implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus using a shallow embedding in the Agda proof assistant. All of our examples parsers have been implemented in this prototype implementation.

I built this website using Forester.
You may search through this site using Ctrl-k.

I am interested in leveraging type theory to develop a programming language that carries intrinsic proofs of parser correctness. That is, if a parser written in such a language compiles then we may guarantee the resulting program is sound with respect to parsing semantics.

In many otherwise verified software developments, the frontend is often unverified or of the final component that is verified. Further, even when they're verified, distinct parser implementations often leverage disparate grammar formalisms. The work spent in one verified development often does not port over nicely to another. Thus, we imagine an extensible, unifying framework to tie together the related (but formally disjoint) efforts found in verified parsing implementations and formal language/grammar theory.

I first worked on this in Intrinsic Verification of Parsers and Formal Grammar Theory in Dependent Lambek Calculus. My own notes and sketches of ongoing work in the same formal system may be found below and throughout this site.
We've been looking to compile the cubical code used for Dependent Lambek Calculus, but it seems that it is infeasible to compile any non-erased cubical.

This is especially problematic, because \epsilon and literals each are encoded with a path type. We may be able to find another strategy to encode them, but it would require moderate refactors. For example, the definition of \epsilon uses a path type. But, we could define a version using the builtin (non-cubical) equality type. Or perhaps a version that pattern matches on the string.

It occurs to me that Greediness as a Predicate on Grammars? may be more accurately characterized as "longest-match" instead of "greediness", but that does not matter too much. A first step is encoding any disambiguation strategy.

Greedy regular expression matching offers a way to break ambiguities introduced by sums and Kleene star. To capture the greedy parsers involve Kleene stars, we may be able to do a much simpler and naive approach.

That is, maybe you can simply restrict the type to make it so the parses following a Kleene star cannot contain a source of ambiguity with respect to that Kleene star. At a first glance, semantically this should enforce the same greediness you'd expect, but I'm not sure how much of this is workable syntactically.
Similarly, you may be able to disambiguate sums by preferring the left summand.

fr:title.text: Greediness as a Predicate on Grammars?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Greediness as a Predicate on Grammars?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: I am not quite sure how to make everything precise, but I believe that greediness may be expressible as a predicate on tensors.

For instance, we may hope to define greediness as something like \mathsf {isGreedy} : A \otimes B \vdash \Omega
\mathsf {isGreedy}~w~(s, a , b) \colonequals \not \exists (s' , a' , b') \in (A \otimes B) w . \mathsf {stringOf}(a) < \mathsf {stringOf}(a')
Where above I mean for w, w' : \mathrm {String}, we define w < w' to mean that w is a proper prefix of w'.
In English, this attempt at a definiton would read as : a parse of A \otimes B is greedy if there is no parse of A \otimes B for the same string where the parse of A occurs over a larger substring.
This definiton cannot work exactly, as it is solely a semantic definiton. Yet it feels close to being workable internally.

fr:title.text: Attempting to Prove Deterministic Regular Expressions are Unambiguous

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Attempting to Prove Deterministic Regular Expressions are Unambiguous

fr:mainmatter.html:p: I can easily show that the \epsilon , literal, \bot , and \oplus of a deterministic regular expression are unambiguous. However, the concatenation case is troubling due to Issues with Unambiguity Definitions.
I have some thoughts about how this could be proven by appealing to some internal proof of finiteness of grammars.

In order to bridge the gap between finite unambiguity and unambiguity, we can try to restrict to grammars that have finitely many parse trees. We'd expect this to address the concern semantically, as that fixes the problem when the parses are interpreted in \mathbf {Set}.

fr:title.text: Sets That Are Isomorphic to Their Own Product

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets That Are Isomorphic to Their Own Product

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X be a set such that X \cong X \times X. Then either X is the empty set, the singleton set, or an infinite set.
We may read this intuitively as stating the fixed points of the squaring operation on cardinals has solutions 0, 1, and all infinite cardinals \kappa .

We can define when a grammar is finite, and then try to prove that finiteness is preserved on some sane operations on grammars. For instance, \And , \oplus , and \to each preserve finiteness. I haven't proven this myself (which would be a useful exercise), but the following is substantiated in any topos with a natural numbers object [johnstone-2002].

fr:title.text: Finite Cardinal Arithmetic in a Topos

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Finite Cardinal Arithmetic in a Topos

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In a topos with a natural numbers object (N, z , s), you can define finite cardinals as objects that arise as the pullback along a morphism p : \top \to N of the generic finite cardinal. Write [p] for the cardinal corresponding to p.

The above characterization is a little obtuse and does warrant some more explanation. One way to make it more concrete is that [z] = \bot and [s \circ n] = \top \oplus [n], and that finite cardinals warrant a nice induction principle. If P is a property expressible in the internal language such that \bot satisfies P, and that whenever A satisfies P then \top \oplus A satisfies P; then every finite cardinal satisfies P. That is, P forms a (z,s)-closed subobject of N and thus P is all of N.
My working mental model is in a presheaf topos, where the natural numbers object can be defined explicity as \Delta (\mathbb {N}) .
The constant presheaf of a set X on a category C is a functor \Delta (X) : C^{op} \to \mathbf {Set} such that
I often call this the discrete presheaf for X, but I don't know if that's standard.
The finite cardinals with respect to \Delta (\mathbb {N}) can be characterized then as,
These obey nice algebraic properties.

The case of \otimes is more problematic. Semantically, for all w : \mathrm {String} we may bound the size of the set of parse trees {\mathopen {}\left \lvert (A \otimes B) w\right \rvert \mathclose {}} \leq \Sigma _{w_{1} \texttt { ++ } w_{2} = w} {\mathopen {}\left \lvert A w_{1}\right \rvert \mathclose {}} {\mathopen {}\left \lvert B w_{2}\right \rvert \mathclose {}}

Precisely knowing this bound isn't too important, but certainly it exists. We could capture this behavior by just adding an axiom that if A and B are each finite, then A \otimes B is finite. Although, I'd rather not add an axiom.

We could directly try to prove that \otimes preserves finiteness. The statment would follow from showing that \otimes preserves monomorphisms. That is, if f : A \hookrightarrow C and g : B \hookrightarrow D, it suffices to show that f \otimes g : A \otimes B \to C \otimes D is a monomorphism. This would imply finiteness, because you may then apply this for C and D as \mathsf {Fin}. However, you would also need to show that \mathsf {Fin} \otimes \mathsf {Fin} is finite, which isn't immediately clear.

In order to bridge the gap between finite unambiguity and unambiguity, we can try to restrict to grammars that have finitely many parse trees. We'd expect this to address the concern semantically, as that fixes the problem when the parses are interpreted in \mathbf {Set}.

fr:title.text: Finite Unambiguity is Not Equivalent to Unambiguity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Finite Unambiguity is Not Equivalent to Unambiguity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For a while I believed finite unambiguity to be equivalent to the other definitions of unambiguity.
Define a grammar A to be finitely unambiguous if A \And A \cong A.
There is likely a better name for this.
A grammar A is unambiguous if the unique map into the terminal object is a monomorphism. That is, A is a subobject of \top .

fr:title.text: Unambiguity as Unique Map into Codomain

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Unambiguity as Unique Map into Codomain

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grammar A is unambiguous if for all grammars B and maps e , e' : A \vdash B we have e = e'.
In a category with terminal objects, this is equivalent to unambiguity defined via subterminality.
A grammar A is unambiguous if the unique map into the terminal object is a monomorphism. That is, A is a subobject of \top .
We may use an analogy from the category of sets, however I had missed the infinite case when translating this idea to grammars.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sets That Are Isomorphic to Their Own Product

We may read this intuitively as stating the fixed points of the squaring operation on cardinals has solutions 0, 1, and all infinite cardinals \kappa .

It is true that if a grammar is unambiguous, then it is finitely unambiguous. However, the converse does not hold unless the grammar has finitely many parse trees for each string. This finiteness condition is a semantic one. If this proof of unambiguity were to be internalized, then it could maybe be captured through the lens of some grammar of finite cardinals.

A is finitely unambiguous but not unambiguous. The isomorphism bewteen A and A \And A amounts to building a bijection between \mathbb {N} and \mathbb {N} \times \mathbb {N}, which is straightforward.
The definitional issues from above can be resolved by a better definition,

fr:title.text: Unambiguity via the Diagonal Being an Isomorphism

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Unambiguity via the Diagonal Being an Isomorphism

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Finite unambiguity does not serve as an adequate definition of unambiguity that is equivalent to [sss-001T] and [sss-001U]. However, the definition attempted via finite unambiguity can be refined to something that is equivalent to these.
A grammar A is unambiguous if \Delta : A \vdash A \And A is an isomorphism. Equivalently, A is unambiguous if \pi _{1} : A \And A \vdash A and \pi _{2} : A \And A \vdash A are equal.
However, this doesn't necessarily help proofs of unambiguity. For instance, proving that sequentially unambiguous A and B, each of which are unambiguous, form an unambigous tensor.
I can show A \otimes B \cong (A \And A) \otimes (B \And B) \cong (A \otimes B) \And (A \otimes B) but this isomorphism isn't carried by \Delta , so this isomorphism doesn't prove unambiguity.

fr:title.text: Star Continuity is a Semantic Property

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Star Continuity is a Semantic Property

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Star continuity in Dependent Lambek Calculus can often be a convenient proof technique, but its important to remember that this shouldn't be the first line of defense.

Star continuity holds in the Agda model, but does it hold in the syntactic model? I believe that it does because of the presence of the indexed coproducts. So perhaps it isn't so sinister after all. It is worth noting that much of the reason performed by inducting on the length of a Kleene star isn't very elegant. If a proof necessitates star continuity, then it doesn't seem to be aided greatly by the type system.

In Wrong Definition of FollowLast, I mention that the definition of follow last sets in the Agda formalization needs to be changed to match the definitions used in [krishnaswami_typed_2019] and [bruggemannkleinwood].
Instead I had define follow last sets as

The followlast set (\mathsf {FLast}(\cdot )) of a grammar A are all the characters that may follow a word in the language of A in a string that is in the language of A.
\mathsf {FLast}(A) = \{ c ~|~ \exists w , w_A . w_A \in L(A) \land w_Acw \in L(A) \}
This definition is encoded in Dependent Lambek Calculus as follows,

The followlast set of a grammar A may be captured in Dependent Lambek Calculus via the following proposition:
c \not \in \mathsf {FLast}(A) := A \And (A \otimes \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes \top ) \vdash \bot

It turns out the original definitions I used aren't incorrect, instead the follow last set of a disjunction must be augmented. In A typed, algebraic approach to parsing and Deterministic regular languages, the follow last sets of a disjunction obey a very aesthetic equality, \mathsf {FLast}(A \oplus B) = \mathsf {FLast}(A) \cup \mathsf {FLast}(B)
However, with my augmented definition if either of A or B is nullable, the follow last set of A \oplus B must also be unioned with \mathsf {First}(A) \cup \mathsf {First}(B).
Until now I had been using the wrong definition of follow last sets. Rather than what I intially had,

The followlast set (\mathsf {FLast}(\cdot )) of a grammar A are all the characters that may follow a word in the language of A in a string that is in the language of A.
\mathsf {FLast}(A) = \{ c ~|~ \exists w , w_A . w_A \in L(A) \land w_Acw \in L(A) \}
I should instead require w_A to be empty in \mathsf {FLast}(A) = \{ c ~|~ \exists w , w_A . w_A \in L(A) \setminus \{ \epsilon \} \land w_A c w \in L(A) \}

Or at least that's what they have in Neel's paper. Max believes I should have a more compelling argument for which definition is better/more appropriate, which is fair enough. The best argument I have thus far is that our original definition would break the property that \mathsf {FLast}(A \oplus B) = \mathsf {FLast}(A) \cup \mathsf {FLast}(B)

Previously in Agda we had constructed equalizers in Dependent Lambek Calculus using sigma types. Further, equalizers form subobjects, which may be comprehended as maps from a type into a subobject classifier.

I believe in our formalization we want to generalize this idea to a broader class of subobjects, maybe even all of them. That is, we could define a subobject classifying grammar \Omega . Then we can internally define any predicate on a grammar g via a term p : g \vdash \Omega .

That is, forall w : \mathrm {String} we have \llbracket {\Omega }\rrbracket (w) \colonequals \mathsf {hProp}, and
\llbracket {\mathsf {subgrammar}(g)(p)}\rrbracket (w) \colonequals \mathchoice {\textstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\llbracket {p}\rrbracket (x)}

The code for this is nearly identical to the defintion of equalizers as sigma types, and I have even built a translation of the equalizers code that is defined with this as its foundation. I have not yet tested if either implementation is preferable.

It isn't yet clear how to best expose this sort of construct syntactically. I suppose you could assume some subobject classifying grammar, but then I don't know if you can then reap the benefits of the propositions internally. That is, how do you reflect the proposition that two terms are equal in the internal language of propositions rather than the external one?

If nothing else, this code gives me a reusable interface to axiomatize smaller, sandboxed ways in which I'd like to internalize certain types of propositions (such as "two terms are equal" or "does not begin with the character c").
The hope for this code is that it let's me inductively prove the follow last soundness of Kleene star.

For a grammar A, the Kleene star {A}^{*} is defined as a least-fixed point,
\mu x . \epsilon \oplus {\mathopen {}\left (A \otimes x\right )\mathclose {}}
In Dependent Lambek Calculus, it is derivable that {A}^{*} \cong \mu x . \epsilon \oplus {\mathopen {}\left (x \otimes A\right )\mathclose {}}.

For a grammar A, the Kleene star {A}^{*} is isomorphic to an indexed coproduct.
{A}^{*} \cong \textstyle \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (n : \mathbb {N}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (n : \mathbb {N}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (n : \mathbb {N}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (n : \mathbb {N}\right )\mathclose {}}}}. \textrm {char}^{\otimes n}
That is, we may view the parses of {A}^{*} like a linear list comprising parses of A concatenated together. Further, for each of these lists we may know the precise length.
When viewing Dependent Lambek Calculus as a model of Kleene algebra, this is precisely the statement that star continuity holds.
I have been stuck on the proof of follow last soundness for the Kleene star case for a few days. To the point of considering guarded recursion.
I don't exactly understand how guarded recursion works, but I suspect it might be the sort of thing that allows some of these proofs to go through or be simplified.
For instance, the sorts of recursive calls to parsers that aren't structurally recursive, but will be decreasing on the inputted strings.

Also, proofs involving Kleene stars that where I would like to assume the inductive hypothesis on the Kleene star after it has been unrolled once. If I wish to prove follow last soundness for the Kleene star of a deterministic regular expression r,
{r}^{*} \And {\mathopen {}\left ({r}^{*} \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot
when r \And {\mathopen {}\left (r \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot and r \And {\mathopen {}\left (c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot .

The proof reduceds to unrolling each of the {r}^{*} and then showing {\mathopen {}\left (r \otimes {r}^{*}\right )\mathclose {}} \And {\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (r \otimes {r}^{*}\right )\mathclose {}} \otimes c \otimes \top \right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \bot
However, my only strategy for such a proof involves invoking an inductive hypothesis for the {r}^{*} terms which would currently be circular reasoning. Although, because they are unrolled once, I suspect I may be able to make some sort of guarded argument and make each of these {r}^{*} to instead be \triangleright {r}^{*}. Then this would allow me to use the inductive hypothesis?

After boarding this out with Pranav. It seems like a very simple solution using star continuity would let me inductively use hypotheses as they relate to concatenations of r. Then I can tie these together by inducting on the indices of the iterated tensors as referenced by continuity.
I don't think this approach would ever nicely generalize to the context free case, so I still suspect that guarded recursion is the way to go.

For instance, the sorts of recursive calls to parsers that aren't structurally recursive, but will be decreasing on the inputted strings.

In a discussion with Eric, we may have stumbled upon a neat interaction of guarded recursion and linearity.

Could it be the case that guarded recursion in a linear setting would let you recover inductive reasoning? For instance, if I were to build a term of a guarded type in a finitary context, I could not do truly coinductive things. I will necessarily consume all of the input eventually or something like this.

Regular languages can be characterized as finite coalgebras, which has a very similar flavor to this interaction between guardedness and linearity. Deterministic automata arise here coalgebraically, and the coalgebras that happen to be finite are precisely those that are regular (which can already be described inductively). It is unclear if there are confounding factors that make this work out for regular languages, and not more general instances of finitely coinductive things.

The first set of a grammar A may be captured in Dependent Lambek Calculus via the following proposition:
c \not \in \mathsf {First}(A) := A \And (\texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes \top ) \vdash \bot

The followlast set of a grammar A may be captured in Dependent Lambek Calculus via the following proposition:
c \not \in \mathsf {FLast}(A) := A \And (A \otimes \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes \top ) \vdash \bot
